vignette:
Sarah describes her life before last spring as a straight line. At eighteen, she had felt a sense of serene, almost surprising, certainty. She was married to Mark, her high school sweetheart, and they had just signed the lease on their first apartment—a small one-bedroom above a bakery that always smelled of warm bread. She’d been working part-time at a downtown coffee shop, saving up for community college classes in the fall. The line of her life was simple, clear, and pointing forward. She felt adult, capable.

The line shattered on a Tuesday night in April. She was walking the six blocks home from a friend’s house, a walk she’d done a hundred times. She took a familiar shortcut through the small city park, the sound of traffic a comforting hum in the distance. The details from that point on are a collage of sensory fragments, sharp and disjointed. The sudden grip on her arm. The scratchy fabric of a dark wool coat against her face. The smell of stale cigarette smoke and damp earth. She doesn’t talk about the rest of it, not directly. She refers to it only as “the park.”

In the first few weeks after, she tried to force the line of her life to be straight again. She told Mark she was fine, just shaken up. She insisted on going back to work, but the clatter of ceramic mugs and the sudden appearance of customers at her side made her flinch. Male customers with deep voices sent a wave of nausea through her. She started making mistakes, dropping trays, giving the wrong change. After two weeks of near-constant panic, she quit, telling her manager she was ill.

The world outside the apartment began to shrink. The evening was the first thing to go. As soon as the sun would dip below the rooftops, a primal dread would settle in her chest, and she’d check the locks on the door and windows again and again. Soon, the daytime felt no safer. A car door slamming on the street below would send her to the floor, heart hammering against her ribs. She stopped going for walks, then stopped going to the grocery store. Now, six months later, she hasn’t left the apartment in over a month. Mark does all the shopping.

Sleep offers no escape. She fights it until exhaustion overtakes her, because sleep is where the fragments become a film, replaying with excruciating clarity. She often wakes up thrashing, the phantom feeling of rough wool on her skin, the smell of cigarettes so real it makes her gag. Mark tries to hold her, to comfort her, but his touch often feels like a trap. She sees the hurt and confusion in his eyes when she recoils, a fresh wave of shame washing over her. She feels broken, contaminated. The young woman who felt so certain and capable is gone, replaced by a stranger who lives inside her skin.

Most days, she sits on the couch by the window, watching people on the sidewalk below. They walk with an ease she can no longer remember, their bodies relaxed, their faces open to the world. They exist on a plane of safety she can no longer access. The sweet smell of baking bread still drifts up from the shop downstairs, but it no longer smells like home. It smells like a place she is trapped.
